title: Amateur gamedev in too deep
author: Honest_Phone8280
selftext:
I've been working on a game since the start of February, and Im starting to get a little overwhelmed. 

For background, I don't have any real experience with coding other than figuring out how to change a few game's save files in the past by editing a line or two, and by having Claude make me some custom webpage tools in the past. I started making the game as just a silly distraction from a different job, and it sort of snowballed. At first it was essentially just a pretty Screensaver that Claude helped me make with my basic pixel art, and now it's turned into an Oregon Trail-style point & click adventure. I think I just figured out the architecture for how im going to populate my 2d-world with semi-procedural locations, and realizing what I signed myself up for has made me nervous, especially when I see how good some of the games posted here look. If you dont mind, I guess i just want to document my progress so far, as a complete amateur in the world of AI gamedev. 

The project began as a way for me to explore world building in a new way for a setting that ive been wanting to write about for years, with the initial goal to just get the creative juices flowing and maybe come up with a little narrative delivery vehicle in the process. I decided to build the game in the form of a single HTML file, primarily because it's the only thing ive had Claude make for me like this before, so I at least knew how to edit the file and communicate with Claude about some basic things. The first attempt showed me the potential, but i made a lot of design decisions that made it impossible to scale larger, so i decided to rebuild the game around mid-march. I tried to engage with things like Gamemaker, but just couldn't get my mind wrapped around what everything meant in a tool like that. As a result, I seem to have built my own custom game engine. 

To describe things as simply as possible, the player controls a vehicle, and the vehicle is displayed on top of a background. The background has a set scale, and that scale is used to calculate the number of backgrounds needed to portray an area and the speed at which the backgrounds needs to move in order to remain accurate as the vehicle moves and changes speeds, keeping everything in the world consistent even as different things move at different speeds. The scale of these backgrounds also helped me map the overall world map, with locations placed in the world according to which background they align with. 

There's about a dozen different location types that are planned to populate the world, with multiples of each. Instead of authoring each one individually, ive been working on designing a location template system that will let me define everything a location needs to be functional so that i can fill the world with 'template' locarions before customizing them to be unique in tiny ways. There are still things that need to be fleshed out like more quests and procedural NPC sprites, but i finally have what I think is the full picture of what a template entails; defining the location type and associated sprite family, defining the locations layout, its decorations, its interactablility & puzzles, its loot & market tables, its NPCs, and its connected jobs. And I'll need to make a template for every location, along with a minimum of 7 sprites for each location, a minimum of 6 sprites for each NPC body type, i'll need to figure out how to make the economy not be completely unbalanced in real gameplay, and write the dialogue and descriptions to replace most of the placeholders that Claude writes. And a million other things. 

So obviously, ive committed the classic novice gamedev blunder of biting off more than I can chew. Except, I feel like now that I can see the path to the end, long as it might be, its not that I think I can't do it. I make progress every day, making sprites, writing lore, designing quests, and making song loops or sound effects whenever I can. I dont have a problem with AI art, I just would rather be the one to make it since I rely entirely on Claude for writing the code that will present the art (i have designed a lot of the architecture, i just dont know how to implement it in code which is why I work with Claude to make most edits). My anxiety instead comes from the thought that at the end of all this work, it still won't be very good. I love my little game even if it isn't really functional yet, but its a weird passion project from an amateur that only initially planned on making a lore-dump vehicle. Seeing how 'clean' the art and animations and general interactivity looks in professional games just makes me wish I had a broader skillet for a project like this, because I probably wouldn't have tried to build such a big world if I hadn't started with the goal of worldbuilding. It just feels so 'easy' with something like this to make the things I write about into something 'real', and I dont want to give up now that I feel like I can see the big picture clearly. 

Idk what this post is meant to be. Maybe this is what people mean when they say that the last 20% is the hard part. If anyone has any tips for how to plan what gets worked on when, maybe that could help.

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body:
You don't know what this post is meant to be, you don't know what game you're building, and you probably don't know who you are.

Time to figure things out. Making a game is about finishing the game. So start deciding what your game is not and cut cut cut.

replies.author: Turbulent-Armadillo9
replies.body:
Yeah the advice I keep hearing for game dev ai or no is: make a really really small game first. A little bigger next time. If you don’t know what to make just recreate an old arcade game just to learn. 

I’m making a fairly simple platformer. I do think I overscoped but I have a plan and can cut if need be.

replies.author: Honest_Phone8280
replies.body: At least you gave me a good name for a generic NPC

replies.author: kytheon
replies.body: You can take the advice or ignore all the haters and follow your chaotic path.

comments.author: TurnYourBrightsOFF
comments.body: A lot I could touch on here... but I'll discuss your anxiety issue.  Your concern honestly shouldn't be whether the game will end up fun, because if you already built a prototype that's genuinely fun to play, then you already proved the core idea works. If the prototype itself isn't fun, then usually the final game won’t be either.

replies.author: Honest_Phone8280
replies.body: Thanks, that helps me a lot with perspective, actually. There are lots of fun parts, im just in the stage now of getting them to work together properly.

comments.author: fued
comments.body:
Oh it's almost guaranteed to be garbage, you have to real skills in gamedev.

Steven king had 4 finished novels before getting any success.
Angry birds was rovios 52nd game.


It takes a long time before you will have experience to make something good, but you will look back upon these games super fondly and might even remake one of them one day, or use parts from this in future products.

comments.author: PomegranateIcy1614
comments.body: Hey bud. it's always okay to cut your scope down and make something smaller out of the big thing you're working on. We call this an inner loop prototype. Pick a tiny slice. Play with it. Get it fun. Practice. You'll feel way better when you have a thing you can touch.
